title: Emergent Electronic Bond-Order Wave in a Quasi-One-Dimensional Chain
authors: Honghao Wang, Tristan R. Cao, Pedro Schlottmann, Gang Cao
abstract: Collective order is notoriously difficult to stabilize in one dimension, where strong fluctuations suppress symmetry-breaking states. Here we report the emergence of an electronic bond-order wave (BOW) in the quasi-one-dimensional (1D) material Ba9Rh8O24, in which structural bonds become active electronic degrees of freedom that overcome 1D fluctuations to establish long-range order. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction uncovers a striking inversion of inequivalent Rh-Rh bonds across a transition TA = 180 K, where short and long bonds interchange their identities rather than undergoing conventional Peierls dimerization. This bond inversion coincides with a heat-capacity anomaly and a profound reorganization of the dielectric response with strong suppression of dielectric loss upon cooling. The BOW exhibits strongly nonlinear, frequency-dependent I-V characteristics, clockwise hysteresis, and nonvolatile memristive switching. These findings uncover an unprecedented transformation from a dynamic bond liquid to a rigid yet electrically reconfigurable BOW, establishing bond-centered electronic order as a new organizing principle for 1D quantum matter.
summary: This work investigates the emergence of a Bond-Order Wave (BOW) in the 1D material $	ext{Ba}_9	ext{Rh}_8	ext{O}_{24}$, demonstrating that structural bonds become active electronic degrees of freedom. A transition at $T_A \approx 180 	ext{ K}$ is marked by a unique bond inversion and the development of nonvolatile, memory-effect electrical switching. This establishes bond-centered electronic order as a key organizing principle for quantum matter in low dimensions.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is stabilizing collective electronic order in one dimension (1D) against strong thermal fluctuations that typically suppress symmetry-breaking states.
main_result: The authors report the emergence of a Bond-Order Wave (BOW) in $	ext{Ba}_9	ext{Rh}_8	ext{O}_{24}$, characterized by a structural bond inversion across a transition temperature $T_A \approx 180 	ext{ K}$. This transition establishes bond-centered electronic order, leading to nonvolatile memristive switching.
method: The study employs a combination of techniques, including single-crystal X-ray diffraction, heat-capacity measurements, dielectric response analysis, and nonlinear transport measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is the quasi-one-dimensional material $	ext{Ba}_9	ext{Rh}_8	ext{O}_{24}$, which is analyzed in the context of electronic bond order, suggesting a connection to the extended Hubbard model.
key_observables: Bond inversion (short $\leftrightarrow$ long bond interchange), heat-capacity anomaly, suppression of dielectric loss ($\epsilon''$), and nonlinear I-V hysteresis loops with remnant voltage ($V_m$).
important_parameters: Transition temperature $T_A \approx 180 	ext{ K}$; the system operates in a regime where structural bonds become active electronic degrees of freedom.
main_assumptions: The transition is argued to be a condensation from a dynamic bond liquid to a rigid BOW, distinct from conventional Peierls dimerization or purely magnetic ordering.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structural bond inversion across $T_A$, the suppression of dielectric response ($\epsilon'$ and $\epsilon''$) below $T_A$, and the development of characteristic clockwise hysteresis in I-V curves below $T_A$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes anomalies across multiple probes (structural, thermodynamic, dielectric, transport) near $T_A$, building a case that the common origin is the reorganization of the Rh-Rh bond network into a rigid BOW state.
why_interesting: The concept of bond-centered electronic order as a new organizing principle, which can be probed via structural changes and electrical switching, offers an analogy to charge density wave physics but with a distinct structural signature (bond inversion).
